Seventh grade science · Unit 7.5

Photosynthesis & Matter Cycling

A tree can grow to weigh tons, but you never see anyone feed it. Where does all that matter come from? In Unit 7.4 you saw animals burn sugar with oxygen; here plants do the reverse and build sugar from air and water. Test ideas with the Unit 0: How Science Works method, as scientists did when they weighed a growing tree.

Where we left off: Unit 7.4 showed animals burning sugar with oxygen. You may already have learned that plants capture light energy (Unit 1) and that food webs pass energy along (Unit 12). Here plants do the reverse: they build sugar from air and water, and matter cycles through living and nonliving things.

Concept 1 · Making food from light

Plants build sugar from air and water

Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water + light energy → sugar + oxygen, in chloroplasts (green because of chlorophyll). Light energy gets stored in the bonds of sugar.

Analogy

A solar-powered kitchen

Air and water are the ingredients, sunlight is the electricity, chlorophyll is the stove. Sugar is the meal.

Concept 2 · Van Helmont's tree

A tree grows from air

Most of a plant's mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air and water, not from soil. Soil gives small amounts of minerals.

Analogy

The famous willow

In the 1600s van Helmont grew a 2.3 kg willow in 90 kg of soil for five years. The tree weighed 77 kg but the soil lost only about 57 grams. His conclusion: water. Today we know the carbon came from CO₂ too.

Data

Before and after

Kilograms, approximate. This is the logic of conservation of mass from Unit 7.2.

Concept 3 · Two directions

Plants and animals trade gases

Plants make sugar and oxygen by photosynthesis, and do respiration too. Animals use both and give back CO₂. Together they cycle matter.

Analogy

A trading partnership

Plants make sugar and release oxygen; animals eat the sugar (or eat the plants) and breathe out CO₂. Each side makes something the other needs, and no one wins by cutting off the partner. Where it breaks: plants also respire, day and night, so the trade is not perfectly one-way.

Try it

Concept 4 · Food chains

Matter cycles, energy flows through

Matter is recycled (the same atoms again and again); energy flows one way (from sun to organisms to heat). Decomposers return matter to soil and air.

Analogy

Recycling vs. electricity

Matter is like bottles: collected and reused. Energy is like electricity: used and gone as heat, so it needs a constant supply from the sun.

Concept 5 · Following one atom

A carbon atom's journey

Carbon moves between air, plants, animals, soil, ocean, and fossil fuels. Photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration, decay, and burning return it.

Analogy

A traveler with many stops

A carbon atom can be in a leaf today, a rabbit next month, and the air again after the rabbit breathes out.

Try it

Choose the next stop

Data

Time carbon stays

Approximate, log scale. Fossil fuels took millions of years to make but we burn them in decades (Unit 13).

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

A student places a sealed jar containing a plant in a dark closet for a week. Predict what happens to the oxygen and CO₂ and why. Then predict what happens if the jar is in a sunny window.

Show a model answer

In the dark the plant does respiration only, so O₂ decreases and CO₂ increases. In light photosynthesis can be faster than respiration, so O₂ rises and CO₂ falls. Matter is conserved: the same carbon and oxygen atoms move between gas and sugar.

0 of 6 correct

Words to know

photosynthesis
Making sugar and oxygen from CO₂, water, and light.
chlorophyll
Green pigment that captures light.
chloroplast
Organelle where photosynthesis happens.
producer
Organism that makes its own food.
consumer
Organism that eats other organisms.
decomposer
Organism that breaks down dead matter.
carbon cycle
Movement of carbon through Earth systems.
glucose
The simple sugar plants make.
stomata
Tiny leaf pores for gas exchange.
cellular respiration
Releasing energy from sugar with oxygen.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $8): elodea or spinach leaves, baking soda, clear cups, a lamp, bromothymol blue, a sealed jar, a kitchen scale, a coffee filter and iodine (starch test).

  • Concept 1: Float leaf discs in baking-soda water under a light and count the discs that rise.
  • Concept 2: Test a leaf for starch after light and dark.
  • Concept 3: Do the bromothymol blue jar test with elodea in light and dark.
  • Concept 4: Weigh a bean seedling and its soil over weeks (a mini van Helmont).
  • Concept 5: Act out the carbon cycle with dice: each roll sends carbon to a new place.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Plants eat soil." Most mass comes from CO₂.
  • "Plants only photosynthesize; animals respire." Plants do both.
  • "Plants breathe in CO₂ and out O₂ like opposite lungs." It is chemistry in cells.
  • "Energy is recycled." Matter cycles, energy flows.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions. Method link: use van Helmont as a case: hypothesis, variables, controls (Unit 0), and why more evidence changed the conclusion.
